issues.legal_issue: A land acquisition authority may not dispense with the landholder’s hearing merely by invoking urgency when the acquisition process has proceeded slowly and no real urgency is demonstrated.
material_facts: The acquisition was for a new jail, a project considered by the government over several years through committees and administrative steps.
The government took nearly a year between publication of the initial acquisition notification and publication of the declaration that the land was needed.
The State did not dispute that interval, and the record showed a slow pace in processing the acquisition.
The hearing on objections was dispensed with, but there was no categorical finding that holding the hearing would harm the public interest.
issues.conclusion: The State was not justified in dispensing with the hearing on objections under the urgency provision. The acquisition notifications were quashed insofar as they concerned the affected land, without preventing a fresh acquisition proceeding conducted in accordance with law.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5A confers a substantial right to object and be heard, which must be strictly respected when property is taken; it is akin to a fundamental right when read with Article 300-A. Sections 17(1) and 17(2) do not automatically authorize dispensing with the inquiry under Section 5A: Section 17(4) must be separately justified by real urgency. The Court relied on Nandeshwar Prasad v. U.P. Government, Munshi Singh v. Union of India, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Darius Shapur Chennai, Essco Fabs Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Haryana, and Union of India v. Mukesh Hans.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The government initiated a proceeding to acquire land for a public project.
predicates.hearing_dispensed_with: The government omitted the landholders’ opportunity to object and be heard before declaring the land needed.
predicates.prolonged_administrative_delay: The government’s processing of the acquisition proceeded slowly over an extended interval, inconsistent with a need for immediate action.

issues.definition: When a land acquisition proceeding omits the landholders’ hearing and the government’s own processing shows prolonged delay, the urgency waiver is unjustified.

issues.legal_issue: Acquiring land to construct a public jail serves a public purpose, but that purpose does not excuse non-compliance with the law governing acquisition.
material_facts: The existing jail was old, situated in a densely populated area, and overcrowded, with substantially more prisoners than its capacity.
The proposed acquisition was for construction of a replacement jail.
The Court did not decide whether the selected site was preferable to the alternative land asserted to be available.
issues.conclusion: Construction of the jail was in the public interest and land could be acquired for it, but only by strictly following the applicable acquisition procedure.
issues.legal_principle: The meaning of public purpose under Section 3(f) must be understood broadly and consistently with constitutional values, including Part III and the Directive Principles, with attention to public benefit rather than the interests of a particular group at the expense of the wider public. Expropriatory legislation must be strictly construed. The Court relied on Authorised Officer, Thanjavur v. S. Naganatha Ayyar, DLF Qutab Enclave Complex Educational Charitable Trust v. State of Haryana, State of Maharashtra v. B.E. Billimoria, and Chairman, Indore Vikas Pradhikaran v. Pure Industrial Coke and Chemicals Ltd.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The government seeks to acquire land for a public project.
predicates.public_correctional_facility_need: The proposed land is intended for a public jail needed to address the condition or capacity of an existing jail.

issues.definition: When land is acquired for a needed public jail, the acquisition serves a public purpose but must still comply with the governing procedure.
